messages.subject: SEM Model not Converging
messages.subject_clean: SEM Model not Converging
messages.body_plain:
May you please assist me!

My model for SEM is not converging, lavaan is giving me an error  message; Warning message:
In lav_object_summary(object = object, header = header, fit.measures = fit.measures,  :
  lavaan WARNING: fit measures not available if model did not converge.
Background: Initially my odinal data (on likert scale -5) was giving me an error message for non positive definiteness NPD,usisng "WLSMV" as my estimator. I then applied smoothing procedure, and then used the resultant sample covariance matrix to run my model, and which is giving me non-convergence error message. Below is the code i am running and the results coming up.
May you please advise which estimator is the best when running ordinal data using sample cov matrix as well.

trial <- read.csv("GoatsNu.csv")
trialdata <-trial %>% dplyr::select(c("prodcapcommercialbreeds":"fapeensustainability"))

VarHeadings <- c( "Q01", "Q02", "Q03", "Q04", "Q05", "Q06", "Q07",
                  "Q08", "Q09", "Q10", "Q11", "Q12", "Q13", "Q14",
                  "Q15", "Q16", "Q17", "Q18", "Q19","Q20", "Q21",
                  "Q22","Q23", "Q24", "Q25", "Q26", "Q27","Q28",
                  "Q29", "Q30", "Q31", "Q32", "Q33","Q34", "Q35",
                  "Q36", "Q37", "Q38", "Q39", "Q40","Q41")
names(trialdata) <- VarHeadings
colnames(trialdata)
trialdata <- cor.smooth(trialdata, eig.tol=10^-12)
cor.smoother(trialdata,cut=.01)

#Measurement Model
m7a<-'PCap =~ Q01 + Q02 + Q03 +Q04 +Q05+Q06 + Q07
GvP =~ Q08 + Q09 +Q10 +Q11+ Q12 + Q13
FnI =~ Q14 +Q15+ Q16+ +Q17+ Q18
MAO =~ Q19 + Q20 + Q21+Q22+Q23+ Q24
CapD =~ Q25 + Q26 +Q27+Q28+Q29+Q30
MIP=~ Q31+Q32+Q33+Q34+Q35+Q36
FIP =~  Q37 +Q38 +Q39+Q40+Q41
#Constrain variance

# Regressions
FIP ~ GvP + FnI + PCap+ MAO + MIP+ CapD'

ml7a <- sem(m7a, sample.cov = trialdata,sample.nobs = 156, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)
summary(ml7a, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)
semPaths (ml7a, what = "paths", whatLabels = "par")

Results are shown in pictures here attached;

I am also suspecting collinearity is the problem and I do not know how to deal with it, I am still new to SEM and lavaan.

Please kindly help.

messages.subject: Re: SEM Model not Converging
messages.subject_clean: SEM Model not Converging
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Instead of applying a smoother, you should try to understand why the covariance matrix is nonpositive definite. Non-positive definiteness means that at least one of the variables either does not have variance or is perfectly predicted by other variables. This may occur because of data preparation error. Inspect the variance and for example regress each indicator on all others one at a time.

Another thing that I see is that the FIP factor seems really weird. Are the indicators correlated? If the indicators are not correlated, then the factor vanishes and the model cannot be estimated. I suggest estimating just a model for FIP to see if that converges. If not, inspect the covariances. If they are low, the factor does not exist and you need to rethink your model.

I taught a short class about model convergence last spring. If you are new to model non-convergence, you might find the materials useful:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4_ip9F8EpVs&list=PL6tc6IBlZmOVpqQ94Oy6OouHHZ2QNGXRQ

The first is just a general intro and the second video goes to the topic. I used stata for the examples, but what I explain applies to R as well.

Mikko

messages.subject: Would the following be possible in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: Would the following be possible in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am currently considering using SEM for one of my PhD projects. I have three waves of data on employee-supervisor dyads and aim to estimate a mediation model. I would like to estimate a Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM; Hamaker, Kuiper, & Grasman, 2015) to separate between effects (between the dyads) from within effects (over time). Given that the same supervisor appears in multiple dyads, I would like to estimate a multi-level model, with level: 1 the dyad level, and level: 2 the supervisor level. I believe that currently multi-level SEM is only possible with two levels, random intercept only. I want to know if the random intercept introduced in a RI-CLPM makes it so one cannot specify a multi-level model anymore. Lastly, I would also like to include a number of covariates. I believe all of these options are possible separately, but could one combine them?

That is, would it be possible to do multi-level mediation using a RI-CLPM, with covariates?

Best,
Wout

Dear professor Shu Fai (and all the community of the lavaan group), thank you very much for your help.

I have another question: I would like to make a sensitivities analysis. For example, I would like to constrain the loading of V1 in F1 =~ V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 to 0 (include or not include V1 in the latent variable F1).
For example, if I write F1 =~= 0*V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 the model run, but I need to define externally to the model a trigger that randomly assumed value 0 or 1 such as:

trigger = sample(c(0,1),1)
model = 'F1 =~= trigger*V1 + V2 + V3 + V4
                 .....'

This code doesn't produce the correct results ... Is there a way to make the correct result?

Thank you very much again for your help,
Best,
Alessio.

messages.subject: Re: lavaan and censored variables
messages.subject_clean: lavaan and censored variables
messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot for the clarifying answer, Terrence!
(Yes, I've noticed speed problems, for instance when using blavaan. Your answer was particularly helpful because it made clear that some limitations will remain.)

On Thursday, 23 February 2023 at 22:14:03 UTC+1 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I would like to use this opportunity to send a warm thank to people like Yves Rosseel,  Terrence D. Jorgensen, and Ed Merkle (and many others) for their work on lavaan and associated packages. Your doing the community a great service!
>
> Thanks for the high praise :-)
>
> > Obviously, lavaan has been through substantial developments in recent years, but I'm not sure which limitations remain.
>
> You can find a list of features and (tentative) plans for future developments on the home page:
>
> https://lavaan.ugent.be/features.html
>
> https://lavaan.ugent.be/development.html
>
> > Is declaring factor indicators (or manifest variables in general) as censored not available in lavaan?
>
> No, and highly doubtful.  lavaan's models all assume normality at some level (e.g., normality of latent responses underlying ordinal variables, or ML estimation of continuous data assuming normality, followed by corrections for violations thereof).  Mplus uses numerical integration to estimate models that do not rely on assuming normality (e.g., Poisson or negative-binomial distributed data).  I've seen papers implementing models for censored data in Mplus, that work by creating a binary (over the hurdle or not) and continuous (missing on the other side of the hurdle) copy of each censored variable, but that also requires numerical integration.  Numerical integration is unpardonably slow in R, so it is just not a feasible option.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject: Re: Multiple mediation analysis with dichotomous outcome
messages.subject_clean: Multiple mediation analysis with dichotomous outcome
messages.body_plain:
Jasper,
This is an interesting aspect of implicit threshold models.  Here is the strategy that I would otherwise follow to investigate that question:

lavaanify(multipleMediation) # list parameters
foo <- sem(multipleMediation, do.fit=FALSE, ordered = c("suic_groups_M2fil_aR"))
lavInspect(foo, what='free') # fixed parameters appear as zero
lavInspect(foo, what='start') # start values of parameters

However, this can be misleading with implicit threshold models because the code that auto-generates the threshold model is apparently not triggered this way.  So, with an implicit threshold model, it seems a better strategy to proceed as follows.

bar <- simulateData(model=multipleMediation, ordered = c("suic_groups_M2fil_aR"))
str(bar)# ordered variable simulated as continuous
summary(bar[,1]) # See distribution
bar[,1] <- cut(bar[,1], breaks=2) # dichotomize ordered variable
baz <- sem(multipleMediation, data=bar, ordered = c("suic_groups_M2fil_aR")) # fit model
summary(baz)
lavInspect(baz, what='free')
lavInspect(baz, what='start')

Here you can see that the threshold model has been implemented as intended.

Here are a few minor things that caught my eye:
1.  You used a different model in your fit from the one you defined.
2.  You can make the total calculation more readable by replacing the products with the  previously defined indirect# parameters.  This will produce the same result.

total := c + indirect1 + indirect2 ...

3. If you desired, you could also define a parameter as the sum of the indirect effects omitting c to obtain inferential statistics for that.  Just be aware that effects in opposite directions can cancel one another out.  A chi-square difference test might offer a more accurate omnibus test in any event.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am conducting multilevel mediation analyses in lavaan, and had been using code passed down to me that didn't specify level blocks, and I didn't realize I needed to until reading through the conversations here (I don't know SEM, only stumbled upon the option to use MSEM with lavaan for multilevel mediation models!).

My question is, does the code I am using still make sense given the multilevel nature of my data and my level-1 (within-person) focus?
My data = occasions nested within individuals; participants took 3 surveys across 10 days
- 64 participants with at least 9 complete days of data each (i.e., complete = all 3 surveys completed that day)
- data is formatted such that N rows = N days for each participant, 1 day per row
- My main focus and RQs are at level 1 or within-persons, the only level 2 variables are between-persons control variables
- The level 2 controls are repeated down all of an individual's rows
- I have 1 predictor (X), 3 partial mediators (M1, M2, M3), and 1 outcome (Y)
- I have 5 control variables = four are level 2 (demographics = control1-control4), and one is level 1 (morning level of Y = AM.Ycontrol)

Below is the code I have been using:
model <-
"M1 ~ a1 * X + control1 + control2 + control3 + control4
M2 ~ a2 * X + control1 + control2 + control3 + control4
M3 ~ a3 * X + control1 + control2 + control3 + control4
Y ~ b1*M1 + b2*M2 + b3*M3 + c*Y + control1 + control2 + control3 + control4 + AM.Ycontrol
ind_eff1 := a1 * b1
ind_eff2 := a2 * b2
ind_eff3 := a3 * b3"
fit <- sem(model = modela, data = TDAT, se = "boot", bootstrap = 1000)
parameterEstimates(fita, boot.ci.type = "bca.simple", rsquare = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, zstat=TRUE, output = "pretty")

I also ran these regressions piecemeal using the mediate function in lme4 and get similar results across both methods.
But based on what I've seen here, the code above wouldn't allow lavaan to automatically separate the within and between components of my level 1 variables. But would using the above code with group-mean (person-mean) mediators and DV, instead of the currently uncentered, effectively remove the between-person variance of level 1 variables (which I want) while still controlling for the level 2 control vars?

Or do I instead need to use the level-specifying block code?
If so, would this be the correct code to use?
model <- '
level: 1
#direct effects
Y ~ b1*M1 + b2*M2 + b3*M3 + c*Y + control1 + control2 + control3 + control4 + AM.Ycontrol

#indirect effects

level:2
#direct effects
Y ~ b1*M1 + b2*M2 + b3*M3 + c*Y + control1 + control2 + control3 + control4 + AM.Ycontrol

#mediator model
M1 ~ a1*X + control1 + control2 + control3 + control4 + AM.Ycontrol
M2 ~ a2*X + control1 + control2 + control3 + control4 + AM.Ycontrol
M3 ~ a3*X + control1 + control2 + control3 + control4 + AM.Ycontrol

#indirect effects
ind_eff1 := a1 * b1
ind_eff2 := a2 * b2
ind_eff3 := a3 * b3
'
fit.ML1 <- sem(model = MLmodel1,
                 data = TDATw1,
                 cluster = "ID", bootstrap = 1000)

Any help would be so appreciated.
Thanks very much in advance!!

Katie

> Jasper,
> This is an interesting aspect of implicit threshold models.  Here is the strategy that I would otherwise follow to investigate that question:
>
> lavaanify(multipleMediation) # list parameters

messages.body_plain:
Jasper,
I understood your question to be whether your script correctly specified the intended model.  I view that as an important question that everyone should ask and answer as part of any analysis.  So, we need a practical method to answer this question on a routine basis.  The first patch of code illustrates how I address the question as part of my typical work flow.  However, I am somewhat idiosyncratic in that I like to make every parameter explicit in my model specification and always use the lavaan() function rather than the convenience functions to fit models.  Because you were leaving aspects of your model implicit to be filled in by default features, my usual approach did not work for your model.

The second patch of code was meant to suggest a method you could follow to answer the question that would work for the approach that you took to specifying the model.  You will find a list of all the model parameters in a pseudo-output generated by fitting the model to the simulated data.  That can serve the same purpose as the parameter table, checking that all and only the expected parameters are present.  You can also get a sense from the presence of standard errors which are free and which are fixed.  The last two lines supplement this by allowing you to check your model in matrix form.  The first line will display all the free parameters so that you can confirm they are where they should be.  The second line allows you to confirm the values of fixed parameters, which are equal to their start values.  You can ignore the start values for free parameters for purposes of model specification checking.

That procedure should allow you to catch most model specification errors as part of your routine work flow.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Re: Scaled vs Unscaled chi-square values
messages.subject_clean: Scaled vs Unscaled chi-square values
messages.body_plain:
Dear Yves,

Based on our last conversation I have a follow-up question:

You mentioned, that all statements about robust RMSEA and CFI from MLM also apply to MLR.

In a paper from Brosseau-Liard & Savalei (2014). Adjusting incremental fit indices for nonnormality I read that in the case of the corrected RMSEA and CFI used in MLM the typical cutoff values from normal ML estimation also apply for these corrected RMSEA and CFI results.

As we discussed that MLM and MLR use the same formulas to calculate RMSEA and CFI and only differ in the scaling beforehand, does this mean that for MLR it is also true that normal cutoff values originally developed from ML estimation can be used? I searched for a paper but couldn't find one.

And what about especially the use of the cutoff values in the case of using MLR or MLM with categorical data (e.g. 5 categories)? Is there anything or any difference between the methods to be aware of?

I am sorry that this is more a general question than a specific lavaan question and I know that cutoff values in general are criticized. But hopefully the answer here also helps future researchers using lavaan.

Thank you very much and best regards

Tobias

Tobias Krieger schrieb am Donnerstag, 5. Januar 2023 um 19:04:38 UTC+1:
> Dear Yves,
>
> Thank you so much for taking the time to answer all my questions, this was incredibly helpful to me.
>
> All the best,
> Tobias
>
> yros...@gmail.com schrieb am Mittwoch, 4. Januar 2023 um 11:16:43 UTC+1:
> > On 1/2/23 18:13, Tobias Krieger wrote:
> > > *The implementation of the Savalei 2021 method for WLSMV. *
> > > Do I understand it correctly that conditional.x = FALSE means, that
> > > models are currently not allowed to have exogenous categorical
> > > covariates to estimate the Savalei 2021 method for WLMSV?
> >
> > conditional.x = TRUE (which is the default if you have categorical data
> > AND exogenous 'x' covariates) means that we first regress out the 'x'
> > covariates, and the main analysis is then based on the *residual*
> > correlation matrix of the endogenous categorical variables (See Muthen 1984)
> >
> > And indeed, conditional.x = TRUE is not supported yet for the
> > computation of the robust RMSEA/CFI when data is categorical. In fact,
> > it only works (for now) if all data is categorical.
> >
> > > If we look at the case where we have _complete and non-normal _data:
> > > 1. Did I understand you correctly, that you in general recommend MLR as
> > > the estimator of choice (in the case of a ML estimator)
> >
> > No. There is nothing wrong with MLM. MLR has the advantage that it can
> > be combined with missing = "ml". For both MLM and MLR, there is a
> > correct 'robust' version of CFI and RMSEA available.
> >
> > > Having both would not be possible with MLMV as you mentioned before.
> >
> > MLMV could be used as well (for complete data only). The only difference
> > is that the test statistic is now using a mean and variance (hence 'MV')
> > adjusting correction (ie test = "scaled.shifted")
> >
> > > 2. But wouldn't it also be possible with MLM to have a correction for
> > > non-normality and a correct robust RMSEA/CFI?
> >
> > Sure.
> >
> > > 3. Are there additional reasons why especially MLR should be recommend?
> >
> > It is can be combined with missing = "ml", that is all.
> >
> > > 4. Also in the case of complete data, I would just use the standard
> > > settings that are automatically implied by MLR, meaning: test =
> > > "yuan.bentler.mplus", se = "robust.huber.white", information =
> > > "observed", observed.information = "hessian", h1.information =
> > > "structured", correct?
> >
> > Yes. See this paper for an overview:
> >
> > https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10705511.2021.1877548
> >
> > (I saw in one of your older presentations that
> > > lavaan would normally use "robust.mlm" in the case of complete data page
> > > 32 <https://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/lavaan2.pdf>, but this is
> > > probably from an older lavaan version as I couldn't find further
> > > information about that)
> >
> > Indeed. That document is 10 years old. (I only keep it there because
> > some papers cite this link.) The Savalei & Rosseel paper above is the
> > better reference. "robust.mlm" is now called "robust.sem", while
> > "robust.mlr" is now called "robust.huber.white". Both refer to the way
> > 'robust' standard errors are computed.
> >
> > > 4. Is there a paper explaining how the robust RMSEA/CFI are calculated
> > > for MLR?
> >
> > It is the same as for MLM. MLM and MLR differ in the way they compute
> > the 'scaling factor' that is used to 'scale' the original test
> > statistic. But once you have this value, the formulas for computing the
> > robust RMSEA/CFI are the same.
> >
> > The case of MLMV is different, hence a different paper.
> >
> > > that means that all statements about robust RMSEA/CFI
> > > in the case of MLM also apply for MLR?
> >
> > Yes.
> >
> > > So the only reason why they
> > > produce slightly different values is not due to formulas but due to the
> > > beforehand corrected data that enters the formulas?
> >
> > Indeed. If data is complete, the main differences are a follows:
> >
> > - MLM implies test = "satorra.benter", using (per default) information =
> > "expected", h1.information = "structured"
> >
> > - MLR implies test = "yuan.benter.mplus", using (per default)
> > information = "observed", observed.information = "hessian", and
> > h1.information = "structured"
> >
> > The meaning of these options is explained in the Savalei & Rosseel
> > (2022) paper.
> >
> > Yves.

> > > 'robust' standard errors are computed.
> > >
> > > > 4. Is there a paper explaining how the robust RMSEA/CFI are calculated
> > > > for MLR?
> > >
> > > It is the same as for MLM. MLM and MLR differ in the way they compute
> > > the 'scaling factor' that is used to 'scale' the original test
> > > statistic. But once you have this value, the formulas for computing the
> > > robust RMSEA/CFI are the same.
> > >
> > > The case of MLMV is different, hence a different paper.
> > >
> > > > that means that all statements about robust RMSEA/CFI
> > > > in the case of MLM also apply for MLR?
> > >
> > > Yes.
> > >
> > > > So the only reason why they
> > > > produce slightly different values is not due to formulas but due to the
> > > > beforehand corrected data that enters the formulas?
> > >
> > > Indeed. If data is complete, the main differences are a follows:
> > >
> > > - MLM implies test = "satorra.benter", using (per default) information =
> > > "expected", h1.information = "structured"
> > >
> > > - MLR implies test = "yuan.benter.mplus", using (per default)
> > > information = "observed", observed.information = "hessian", and
> > > h1.information = "structured"
> > >
> > > The meaning of these options is explained in the Savalei & Rosseel
> > > (2022) paper.
> > >
> > > Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Latent Variable with Two Indicators
messages.subject_clean: Latent Variable with Two Indicators
messages.body_plain:
> The construct is measured at both time points. Do I constrain both indicators to one

The loadings?  Yes, so that the factor variance is freely estimated on both occasions.  Also correlate each indicator's residuals across time.

> and the intercept of both indicators to zero?

No, 2-indicator factors do not have the same identification issue for the mean structure, only the covariance structure.  You can estimate both intercepts and fix the latent means to zero.  If you are interested in comparing the latent mean between the 2 occasions, then you have to test scalar invariance by equating the Time-1 and Time-2 intercepts, so you can free the Time-2 factor mean.  Metric invariance is implied by the loadings all being 1, and it is not a testable assumption with only 2 indicators.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> If I add a newdata to get the predicted response variables from different values of my explanatory variables it gives me the exact same results as when I don't use a new dataset.

Can you provide a reproducible example?

> The example on the package documentation uses latent variables but I don't have any, I don't know if it works only for them.

It does:

set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(15)
dat <- data.frame(x = x, y = x + rnorm(15))
newdat <- data.frame(x = seq(-1, 1, 0.5), y = NA)

fit <- sem("y ~ x", data = dat)
lavPredictY(fit) # predictions for observed data
lavPredictY(fit, # predictions for new data
            newdata = newdat)

messages.subject_clean: Would the following be possible in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
> the same supervisor appears in multiple dyads

So you have a "many-with-1" design?

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8324320/

Then is your CLPM a longitudinal actor-partner interdependence model (APIM)?

> I would like to estimate a multi-level model, with level: 1 the dyad level, and level: 2 the supervisor level. I believe that currently multi-level SEM is only possible with two levels, random intercept only. I want to know if the random intercept introduced in a RI-CLPM makes it so one cannot specify a multi-level model anymore.

That is not a problem.  You are handling your nesting of repeated measures within subjects/dyads via wide-format (like growth-curve modeling), so the model you describe is still only 2 levels (dyads within supervisors).
The level-1 effects are how supervisors behave with specific employees (and vice versa), relative to how they behave with all their employees on average
The level-2 effects are how supervisors behave with all employees on average (and vice versa)

> Lastly, I would also like to include a number of covariates. I believe all of these options are possible separately, but could one combine them?

Yes, that's possible.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: multilevel SEM - specifying levels?
messages.subject_clean: multilevel SEM - specifying levels?
messages.body_plain:
> does the code I am using still make sense given the multilevel nature of my data and my level-1 (within-person) focus?

I think it is unlikely that your Level-1 residuals are independent, given they are repeatedly measured on the same individual.  Autocorrelated Level-1 covariance structure is more plausible, but not possible in MLSEM with lavaan (or lme4 for that matter), but is available in nmle.  It is possible using wide-format data in lavaan (so it is a single-level SEM, using a (RI-)CLPM), but you might have trouble due to the small Level-2 sample size.

> - I have 5 control variables = four are level 2 (demographics = control1-control4)

So those should only appear in the level: 2 model

> one is level 1 (morning level of Y = AM.Ycontrol)

Are they the same for everyone?  If there is no Level-2 variance, or if you don't want a person-mean-centered interpretation of this predictor, then you can just specify them in the level: 1 model (in which case lavaan would not decompose that variable into latent Level-1 and -2 components).

> the code above wouldn't allow lavaan to automatically separate the within and between components of my level 1 variables

Correct, not to mention your SEs and test statistics would not be robust to the violated independence assumption.  Unless you declared cluster = "ID" to request cluster-robust SEs and tests for your single-level model.  But then you wouldn't be able to answer research questions at Level 2.

> Or do I instead need to use the level-specifying block code?

That tells lavaan to run a MLSEM.  Any variables declared in both models (i.e., at each level) will be decomposed in the "latent" way, which can be more robust when cluster means have a lot of sampling error.

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/a0012869

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/a0024376

But this means you need to use the uncentered variables in your MLSEM, so the decomposition happens implicitly during estimation.

> If so, would this be the correct code to use?

No, remove the Level-2 predictors from the Level-1 model (maybe also vice versa; see my comment above about covariates).
Also, use different parameter labels across levels, so you don't make the ecological/atomistic fallacy.
If you are interested in estimating contextual effects, you can add user-defined (differences between) any analogous parameter across levels.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: LGM: Estimating effect on slope for specific variable at post measurement
messages.body_plain:
> a latent growth model to analyse data of an intervention study with three measurement time points

>From your description below ("post-measurement"), this sounds like a pretest, posttest, follow-up design.  A linear growth model is probably not appropriate for that.  You generally expect a pre-post change, then either no change at follow-up or (often) diminished effect (so closer to pretest level, i.e., "growth" in the opposite direction).

Perhaps a latent difference score (LDS) model is more appropriate, in which case you can regress the latent difference scores (changes) on covariates.
Or investigate "residualized change" by regressing both posttests on the pretest (as well as covariates) and looking for (adjusted) mean differences to test whether posttest levels are consistent.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan Team,

I am Priyanka Pereira, a PhD candidate at the University of Twente in The Netherlands. I have just used Lavaan to conduct a confirmatory factor analysis. Everything went well. Thank you very much for this easy-to-use package!

I would now like to use the factor scores to do the following:
Find the mean and standard deviation for each factor
Evaluate the prediction of a certain factor by a few of the other factors
Investigate the (possible) latent classes among the respondents

I have used the lavPredict function to obtain the factor scores. However, when I calculate the correlations between these factor scores, they do not match the correlations obtained from the summary of the model.

Therefore, I have a few questions:
Can the lavPredict function handle ordinal data?
Are the correlations calculated using the factor scores? If yes, how are these factor scores calculated?
I understand that the factor scores from the lavPredict function are calculated as the sum of each item multiplied by its respective factor score weight: Sum (Item1Score x Item1FactorScoreWeight + Item2Score x Item2FactorScoreWeight + …). Is this understanding correct?
If the answer to question 2 is yes, is it acceptable for me to have one set of factor scores (from the summary of the model) for the correlations between the factors, and another set of factor scores (from the lavPredict function) for the three points listed above?
Unfortunately, the factor scores obtained via the lavPredict function are like z scores. How can I use these to continue with the three points listed above? For example, the mean of each factor turns out to be (close to) 0.

Thank you very much for your time and guidance!

Kind regards,
Priyanka Pereira

messages.subject_clean: Factor Scores in Lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Priyanka--
     If you want factor means and variances, there are model parameter estimates that provide those. The "factor scores" that lavaan provides do not actually match the factors themselves. Actual factor scores must include an additional arbitrary component due to the phenomenon of factor indeterminacy. Basically, the factors are underdetermined by the data. See, for example, Grice (2001):
Grice, J. W. (2001). Computing and evaluating factor scores. Psychological methods, 6(4), 430.
     This documentation page answers your question about ordinal data:
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/lavaan/html/lavPredict.html
     The means and variances of common factors are arbitrary--the factors are statistical fabrications with no actual existence, so their moments only have values relative to something else. If you don't want the means to be 0, add something to them. In a multiple group model, means in some groups will be relative to means in other groups. Variances are similarly arbitrary.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Differing behaviour between Mplus an lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Differing behaviour between Mplus an lavaan
messages.body_plain:
I am running an ALT-SR model with no constraints. I am seeing some quite different behaviour between Mplus and R. The code for both are now from Mund and Nestler supplement section to help isolate what is happening (https://osf.io/sjph7/).

 Mplus (v8.8) terminates normally with fit tests:

·      Chi-Square: 681.638, p-value 0.0000
·      RMSEA: 0.044
·      CFI/TFI: 0.998 / 0.988

Running this same code using the command (lavaan v0.6.13): mplus2lavaan("altsr.inp"). This gives a warning: some estimated lv variances are negative. The parameter estimates are quite different. The same fit tests are:

·         Chi-Square: 7403.039, p-value 0.0000
·         RMSEA: 0.145
·         CFI/TFI: 0.989 / 0.922

Running the R code: sem(altsr, data = D,  missing = "FIML"). This gives a warning: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found! And, summary() warns:

lavaan 0.6.13 did NOT end normally after 2967 iterations

** WARNING ** Estimates below are most likely unreliable

And, consequently no fits tests are reported.

I have searched for why this different behaviour might occur but would be grateful if anyone was able to suggest how I can overcome this. The dataset has 88, 958 observations with some missing data.

messages.subject: Re: Theshold model
messages.subject_clean: Theshold model
messages.body_plain:
> When "Threshold and loadings" model has been confirmed, Can I compare the means  between groups?

No, means are not comparable without (at least partial) scalar invariance (i.e., equal thresholds, loadings, and intercepts for a majority of the construct's indicators).  Wu & Estabrook (2016) is an invaluable resource.

https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0

> FYI, "Thrreshold,loading, intercept model"  did not met.
>
> Simply, what implications in this case?

You can try to identify a partial invariance model by freeing the intercepts for one indicator at a time.  There are more robust methods described in other posts you can find on this forum, but that is a good start.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Would the following be possible in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: Would the following be possible in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
I indeed have a many-with-1 design, with supervisors rating their employees, and vice versa. I aim to assess the impact of a supervisor's directive leadership style (rated by the employee) on an employee's performance and creativity (rated by the supervisor). Eventually I would also look at contextual determinants of directive leadership to make it a mediation model.

But taking it step by step, I started with the second step of the mediation, and tried to add covariates to a RI-CLPM. I used the riclpmr package to generate lavaan syntax, and I manually added covariates by regressing the observed variables on the covariates (constrained over time; based on Mulder & Hamaker, 2021). This is the lavaan model I came up with:

"
ri_w =~ 1*W1_E_Directive + 1*W2_E_Directive + 1*W3_E_Directive
ri_x =~ 1*W1_Perf + 1*W2_Perf + 1*W3_Perf
ri_y =~ 1*W1_Crea + 1*W2_Crea + 1*W3_Crea
ri_w ~~ ri_w
ri_x ~~ ri_x
ri_y ~~ ri_y
ri_w ~~ ri_x + ri_y
ri_x ~~ ri_y
W1_E_Directive ~ W1_E_Directive_mu*1
W2_E_Directive ~ W2_E_Directive_mu*1
W3_E_Directive ~ W3_E_Directive_mu*1
W1_Perf ~ W1_Perf_mu*1
W2_Perf ~ W2_Perf_mu*1
W3_Perf ~ W3_Perf_mu*1
W1_Crea ~ W1_Crea_mu*1
W2_Crea ~ W2_Crea_mu*1
W3_Crea ~ W3_Crea_mu*1
lat_w1 =~ 1*W1_E_Directive
lat_w2 =~ 1*W2_E_Directive
lat_w3 =~ 1*W3_E_Directive
lat_x1 =~ 1*W1_Perf
lat_x2 =~ 1*W2_Perf
lat_x3 =~ 1*W3_Perf
lat_y1 =~ 1*W1_Crea
lat_y2 =~ 1*W2_Crea
lat_y3 =~ 1*W3_Crea
lat_w1 ~~ lat_x1 + lat_y1
lat_w2 ~~ r_wx*lat_x2 + r_wy*lat_y2
lat_w3 ~~ r_wx*lat_x3 + r_wy*lat_y3
lat_x1 ~~ lat_y1
lat_x2 ~~ r_xy*lat_y2
lat_x3 ~~ r_xy*lat_y3
lat_w2 ~ w_w*lat_w1 + w_x*lat_x1 + w_y*lat_y1
lat_w3 ~ w_w*lat_w2 + w_x*lat_x2 + w_y*lat_y2
lat_x2 ~ x_w*lat_w1 + x_x*lat_x1 + x_y*lat_y1
lat_x3 ~ x_w*lat_w2 + x_x*lat_x2 + x_y*lat_y2
lat_y2 ~ y_w*lat_w1 + y_x*lat_x1 + y_y*lat_y1
lat_y3 ~ y_w*lat_w2 + y_x*lat_x2 + y_y*lat_y2
lat_w1 ~~ lat_w1
lat_w2 ~~ e_w*lat_w2
lat_w3 ~~ e_w*lat_w3
lat_x1 ~~ lat_x1
lat_x2 ~~ e_x*lat_x2
lat_x3 ~~ e_x*lat_x3
lat_y1 ~~ lat_y1
lat_y2 ~~ e_y*lat_y2
lat_y3 ~~ e_y*lat_y3

# New code added:
# https://jeroendmulder.github.io/RI-CLPM/lavaan.html#Ext_1:_time-invariant_predictor
# Control for W1 Covariates at W1, W2, W3

On Wednesday, March 8, 2023 at 9:57:23 AM UTC+1 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > When "Threshold and loadings" model has been confirmed, Can I compare the means  between groups?
>
> No, means are not comparable without (at least partial) scalar invariance (i.e., equal thresholds, loadings, and intercepts for a majority of the construct's indicators).  Wu & Estabrook (2016) is an invaluable resource.
>
> https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0
>
> > FYI, "Thrreshold,loading, intercept model"  did not met.
> >
> > Simply, what implications in this case?
>
> You can try to identify a partial invariance model by freeing the intercepts for one indicator at a time.  There are more robust methods described in other posts you can find on this forum, but that is a good start.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Grace,
Yes, that indicates a problem.  Additional constraints should never improve fit.  Her are some strategies:
1. Check that both models were fit to the same data: same variables and same cases.
2. Try the less constrained model with multiple random start values to see if you are at a local minimum.
3. See if it is possible to test the same constraint in a model with fewer other constraints to optimize the fit of the less constrained model.

Keith

messages.body_plain:
Leonie--
     The warning message--not an error--is actually pretty straightforward. If a set of variables are not redundant, then their covariance matrix will have a positive determinant. Based on your model, the covariance matrix of your common factors does not. This can happen is a variance is negative or if two or more variables have correlations or multiple correlations that are too high--or if the factor model is simply wrong for the data, leading to "impossible" parameter estimates. "Too high" is the immediate issue with your results.
     In the correlation matrix of common factors, you have a correlation (between factors "cognitive" and "physical") estimated as 0.999, so effectively 1. Keep in mind that the conclusion that a matrix has a positive determinant is affected by random sampling variance, so that the very same matrix may be judged "OK" if sample size is large but "not OK" if sample size is small. But a correlation of 0.999 is likely to produce this warning regardless of sample size. Even the 0.999 correlation between the "physical" and "fatigue" factors may be high enough to trigger the warning, at low sample size..
     Keep in mind that you are estimating 57 model parameters using 127 cases, so there may be some instability in your parameter estimates, beyond what is reflected in standard errors.
     Model fit--in the sense of discrepancy between model and data--appears to be good. But the 0.999 correlation suggests that the "physical" and "cognitive" factors are not distinct. To see this more clearly, you might estimate a model where those items all load on a single common factor. If you were hypothesizing that a model with distinct factors was better for your population, these results do not tend to support that position.

messages.subject_clean: RMSEA value in anova and lavTestLRT function
messages.body_plain:
I believe it is simply RMSEA computed using the chi-square difference and model df difference:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-14
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.

# Adapted the example of cfa()
HS.model.1 <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit.1 <- cfa(HS.model.1, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
HS.model.2 <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
                textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
                speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
                visual ~~ 0 * textual + 0 * speed
                textual ~~ 0 * speed'
fit.2 <- cfa(HS.model.2, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)

(lrt <- lavTestLRT(fit.2, fit.1))
#>
#> Chi-Squared Difference Test
#>
#>       Df    AIC    BIC   Chisq Chisq diff   RMSEA Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
#> fit.1 24 7517.5 7595.3  85.305
#> fit.2 27 7579.7 7646.4 153.527     68.222 0.26875       3  1.026e-14 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Compute RMSEA using Chi-square difference and the df difference
rmsea_self <- sqrt(((lrt[2, "Chisq"] - lrt[1, "Chisq"]) - 3) / (3 * nobs(fit.2)))
rmsea_self
#> [1] 0.268752

It is a clinical sample and the items only have three options. Maybe the problem occurred at item level, with some items extremely highly correlated?

You used "ordered". You can lavInspect(), e.g., lavInspect(fit.pcsi8.o, "sampstat") and examine the correlations (estimated from the contingency tables), and then examine the 3x3 contingency tables of item-pairs with high correlations.

messages.body_plain:
This is what I do for similar cases in my work:

mod <- "F1 =~ @trigger@ * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"

new_mod <- function(i) {
    gsub("@trigger@",
         i,
         mod,
         fixed = TRUE)
  }
new_mod(sample(c(0, 1), 1))
#> [1] "F1 =~ 1 * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"
new_mod(sample(c(0, 1), 1))
#> [1] "F1 =~ 0 * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"
new_mod(sample(c(0, 1), 1))
#> [1] "F1 =~ 1 * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"
new_mod(sample(c(0, 1), 1))
#> [1] "F1 =~ 1 * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"

You can name @trigger@ in any way you want. Just make sure that it does not conflict with other words in the model syntax when calling gsub().

Hope this helps.

Regards,
Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝)

Correction: I should have set the mode syntax as an argument. Coding it inside the function definition is fine for internal use, but is not a good practice. Passing the model syntax as an argument also allows us to change the model syntax without the need to redefine the function.

mod <- "F1 =~ @trigger@ * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"

new_mod <- function(i, model) {
    gsub("@trigger@",
         i,
         model,
         fixed = TRUE)
  }
set.seed(87041)
new_mod(sample(c(0, 1), 1), model = mod)

#> [1] "F1 =~ 1 * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"

new_mod(sample(c(0, 1), 1), model = mod)

#> [1] "F1 =~ 1 * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"

new_mod(sample(c(0, 1), 1), model = mod)

#> [1] "F1 =~ 0 * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"

new_mod(sample(c(0, 1), 1), model = mod)

#> [1] "F1 =~ 1 * V1 + V2 + V3 + V4"

Hi everyone,

I'm part of a collective offering summer virtual methods training, the Pittsburgh Summer Methodology Series (PSMS). Many of these workshops use lavaan, and so I'm including details below. I'm happy to field questions anyone might have.

Thanks!
matt

Dear colleagues,

Apologies for the cross-posting…

I’m very pleased to announce the slate of this year’s Pittsburgh Summer Methodology Series <https://www.pittmethods.com/> workshop offerings. These include statistical methods as well as best practices in study design, and are highly relevant for applied research.

This year we are offering all our popular courses from previous years, as well as adding a few new workshops.

This summer’s workshops include:

Introduction to R for Social Scientists

Intermediate R for Social Scientists (NEW)

Equity Informed Measurement

Dyadic Longitudinal Data Analysis (NEW)

Introduction to Structural Equation Modeling

Longitudinal Structural Equation Modeling

Assessing Suicidal and Nonsuicidal Self-Injury

Applied Machine Learning in R

SMART & Pragmatic Clinical Trials

Designing Ambulatory Assessment Studies

Latent Profile Analysis

Latent Transition Analysis (NEW)

Multilevel Modeling for Longitudinal Data

Time-Series Analysis for Intensive Longitudinal Data (NEW)

Group Iterative Multiple Model Estimation (GIMME)

Multilevel Structural Equation Modeling (NEW)

Introduction to Item Response Theory

The full schedule of courses and links to individual descriptions can be found here: https://www.pittmethods.com/courses

We offer special reduced pricing for trainees (graduate students and post-docs), and we’ve resisted the otherwise ubiquitous pressures of inflation! Combining some course registrations provides substantially reduced rates. Here is a link to registration: https://www.pittmethods.com/course-offerings

All courses are offered virtually via Zoom and will be recorded for attendees to continue to reference after the course. Look forward to seeing you in the workshops….

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot Joe!

Στις Πέμπτη 1 Δεκεμβρίου 2022 στις 6:08:31 μ.μ. UTC+1, ο χρήστης bbj...@gmail.com έγραψε:
> You are welcome.  I had some time and wanted to prove a few things to myself.  I used data from Dave Kenny’s website, the analysis of which appears near the end of Kenny et al. (2006).  Code is below.  The MSEM version has some nice advantages but a few drawbacks, too, most notably no obvious way to get residual variances for each partner’s DV.  But the regression estimates and variances are spot on as reported in Kenny et al.
>
> pacman::p_load(tidyverse, lavaan)
>
> #wide file ready for APIM/SEM
> mixdata <- haven::read_spss("http://davidakenny.net/kkc/c7/campbell.sav")
>
> names(mixdata)
> head(mixdata)
>
> #specify model
> apim.sem <- '
> mdistr ~ mneuro + fneuro
> fdistr ~ fneuro + mneuro
>
> mdistr ~ 1
> fdistr ~ 1
>
> mneuro ~~ fneuro
> '
>
> apim.sem.out <- sem(apim.sem, data=mixdata)
> summary(apim.sem.out)
>
> #convert to long file
> mixdata |>
>   pivot_longer(cols = (mdistr:fneuro),
>                names_to = c("gender", ".value"),
>                names_pattern = "(.)(.*)") |>
>   mutate(sex0 = ifelse(gender=="m", 0, 1),
>          male = ifelse(gender=="m", 1, 0),
>          female = ifelse(gender=="f", 1, 0)) |>
>   group_by(dyad) |>
>   mutate(pneuro = sum(neuro)-neuro) |> #get partner score on same line as actor
>   ungroup() |>
>   mutate(act.neuro = sex0*neuro, part.neuro=sex0*pneuro) |> #needed interactions
>   rownames_to_column("id") -> mixdata.long
>
>
> head(mixdata.long)
>
> names(mixdata.long)
>
> apim.msem <- '
>
> level: 1
> distr ~ a*neuro + pa*pneuro + g*sex0 + ap*act.neuro + p*part.neuro
>
> #Compute APIM estimates from regression effects
> act.act := a + pa*0 + g*0 + ap*0 + p*0 #male actor effect
> part.act := a*0 + pa + g*0 + ap*0 + p*0 #female-male partner effect
> act.part := a*0 + pa + g*0 + ap*0 + p #male-female partner effect
> part.part := a + pa*0 + g*0 + ap + p*0 #female actor effect
>
>
> level: 2
> #residual covariance at the between-dyad level
>
> #intercept
> distr ~ 1
> '
>
> apim.msem.out <- sem(apim.msem, cluster = "dyad", data=mixdata.long)
> summary(apim.msem.out)
>
>
> Joe
>
>
>
> > On Nov 29, 2022, at 1:24 AM, john pappas <pappa...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I would like to thank you for your suggestions. They were really helpful cause till now I thought that the two approaches (SEM and MLM) can do exactly the same thing. However, it seems that in some cases and depending on your research question, you need one of them.
> >
> > Thank you so much for your help!
> >
> > Yannis
> > Στις Δευτέρα 28 Νοεμβρίου 2022 στις 10:07:34 π.μ. UTC-8, ο χρήστης bbj...@gmail.com έγραψε:
> > > Probably not with that data format.  Seems this requires a multilevel SEM, with observations nested within dyad in a long-file format—what you have here is the wide file with dyad as the unit of analysis.  See Lederman and Kenny (2017) and work that has followed.
> > >
> > > You’d then use gender as a moderator for your regressions at L1.  L2 would be dyadic variances and covariances, though you can include dyadic-level predictors if desired. lavaan can handle the model pretty easily.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > > On Nov 28, 2022, at 10:53 AM, Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Perhaps you could sort you cases as male buyer vs female buyer and use a multi group approach, constraining some parameters to equality but letting others vary across groups. But you will have to infer some parameters estimates as differences across groups, because genders won't be in the model explicitly

messages.body_plain:
> Is there literature on that?

See the Reference I provided on the ?plausibleValues help page, which has further references (see the ones with Mislevy as (co)author).

https://www.statmodel.com/download/Plausible.pdf

https://www.ierinstitute.org/fileadmin/Documents/IERI_Monograph/IERI_Monograph_Volume_02_Chapter_01.pdf

> make sense to pool this plausible values and use them as factor scores (indicators) in a subsequent analysis (aonther cfa-model)?

No, they are not indicators of a factor.  They are estimates of subjects' level on the latent common factor, so they do not include measurement error.  They still include factor indeterminacy and sampling error.  The way to use them is shown in the first ?plausibleValues help page example (with complete data).  The additional complication of estimating them with multiple imputations of incomplete data is that there are more imputations (i.e., several samples of plausible values drawn from each of multiple imputations).  The last help-page example has 10 imputations of missing data, estimated using cfa.mi(), from which 5 plausible values are sampled from each of 10 imputations.  You would then just analyze your path model using all 10 * 5 = 50 sets of plausible values.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: CFA
messages.body_plain:
Grace,
You cannot justify the better fit.  It is a problem.

If you use the lavaanify() function on your model syntax, you can see the parameter table with a column for start values.
You can use either the start() model syntax to change the start values or directly insert them into the parameter table (and then use that for the model when you estimate the parameters).  I find the second approach a little more convenient but that may be a matter of personal taste.  You can then put the process of choosing start values, inserting them, and fitting the model, into a loop using the for() function.  When I do this, I often use a uniform distribution to choose random start values: e.g., runif(n=1, min=-1, max=1).  This will allow you to re-estimate your parameters from various sets of parameter values to see if the model converges to the same solution.  If you get different solutions, you know that you have a local minimum problem.  In that case, try many sets of start values and choose the solution with the best fit.  With any luck, that will give you a fit that is not worse than the constrained model.  To be safe, you might then run the constrained model with the same start values that you used for the unconstrained fit that you selected.  For convenience, it can useful to save the start values and the index value from the for loop into a list inside the loop (create an empty list before the loop and add to that to avoid recreating it inside the loop and overwriting past information).  However, if it is easier for you, you can just print this information inside the loop and then retrieve it from your console.  This is not a quick fix, it will take some effort, but it is my suggestion for how best to proceed.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Gonzalo--
     Is this annual data for one country? If so, then your annual robservations are not independent observations. It is possible that nonconvergence is due not only to your small sample size but also to the nonindependence of observations. A time series approach would be more appropriate. A partial least squares path modeling approach would not be correct unless it also addressed the non-independence. A least squares ap[proach may well bypass some nonconvergence problems, but you will still have a small sample size, which will make you parameter estimates relatively unstable.

messages.subject: Re: Multiple groups: Can constrain 2 groups to be equal and 1 to vary?
messages.subject_clean: Multiple groups: Can constrain 2 groups to be equal and 1 to vary?
messages.body_plain:
> is there a way to convey this through group.equal argument rather than typing c(a, a, NA) or something similar for every single loading path?

No, group.equal= operates at the level of a parameter, applied across all groups.

> if I find that I have noninvariance comparing the configural model to model with the group.equal = loadings argument, can I do a follow up that would allow me to see if I have invariant loadings for 2 of the 3 groups?  That is, apply group.equal for 2 groups on loadings but allow the 3rd group's loadings to be estimated/unconstrained?

That is an incredibly (Type I and II) error-prone data-driven procedure .  If an item functions differentially, it functions differentially.  I wouldn't recommend fishing around further, just leave it free.  Unless you actually have substantive theoretical reasons to expect 1 group to respond different to that item than the other 2 do.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

On Monday, March 13, 2023 at 1:45:07 PM UTC+1 kma...@aol.com wrote:
> Grace,
> You cannot justify the better fit.  It is a problem.
>
> If you use the lavaanify() function on your model syntax, you can see the parameter table with a column for start values.
> You can use either the start() model syntax to change the start values or directly insert them into the parameter table (and then use that for the model when you estimate the parameters).  I find the second approach a little more convenient but that may be a matter of personal taste.  You can then put the process of choosing start values, inserting them, and fitting the model, into a loop using the for() function.  When I do this, I often use a uniform distribution to choose random start values: e.g., runif(n=1, min=-1, max=1).  This will allow you to re-estimate your parameters from various sets of parameter values to see if the model converges to the same solution.  If you get different solutions, you know that you have a local minimum problem.  In that case, try many sets of start values and choose the solution with the best fit.  With any luck, that will give you a fit that is not worse than the constrained model.  To be safe, you might then run the constrained model with the same start values that you used for the unconstrained fit that you selected.  For convenience, it can useful to save the start values and the index value from the for loop into a list inside the loop (create an empty list before the loop and add to that to avoid recreating it inside the loop and overwriting past information).  However, if it is easier for you, you can just print this information inside the loop and then retrieve it from your console.  This is not a quick fix, it will take some effort, but it is my suggestion for how best to proceed.
>
> Keith
> ------------------------
> Keith A. Markus
> John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
> http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
> Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
> http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
>
>

messages.subject: Time-varying covariates (TCV): Which method to use to scale/mean center a TVC in latent growth models ?
messages.subject_clean: Time-varying covariates (TCV): Which method to use to scale/mean center a TVC in latent growth models ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have longitudinal data across several time points. At each time point, participants completed an online test up to 3 times (i.e., measurements were completed 1-3 times at each timepoint). The number of times a participant repeated the test was optional, with participants generally completing the test more times at baseline.

I plan to run latent growth models using lavaan on this data to model the average test scores over time to look at the trajectories of test performance. However, I would like to take into account the number of times a participant completed a test at a given timepoint. Therefore I plan to include the number of times a participant completed the test at each timepoint as an unconditional time-varying covariate (TVC).

I'm wondering which method of scaling is most appropriate in this circumstance for my TVC (i.e., number of times the test was taken). Mean-centering using:

A) the mean across all timepoints for each participant (i.e., person-mean centered),

B) the mean across all participants and timepoints (i.e., grand-mean centered), or

C) the mean of first time point (or other referent point) across all participants (i.e., group-mean centered/centering within context)?

messages.body_plain:
Grace,
Unless you are being overly modest when you say that you are new to R, it may be best to seek out a colleague who can assist you with this.

1. lavaanify() takes model syntax as a parameter, not a model fit.  See the help file for details.
2. The random distribution is for the parameter, not the data.  It works the same with our without categorical data.
3. Choose a range of values that makes sense for your model.  I could not find my sample code so I modified the lavaan example below.  See the comments inside for explanation.

require(lavaan)
# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example (modified)
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

HS.table <- lavaanify(HS.model,
                      auto.var=TRUE,
                      auto.fix.first=TRUE,
                      auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
HS.table # look and see

myResults <- list() # empty list for use in loop
nReps <- 15 # change to what you want

# Caution: This may take some time depending on value of nReps.
for(r in 1:nReps){
  lambdaStart <- runif(n=4, min=-2, max=2) # four values
  lambdaStart1s <- c(1, lambdaStart[1:2], 1, lambdaStart[3:4]) # insert fixed
  #lambdaStart1s # look and see

  new.HS.table <- HS.table
  new.HS.table$ustart[1:6] <- lambdaStart1s # insert start values
  #new.HS.table # look at ustart column

  fit <- lavaan(new.HS.table, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
                auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
                auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)

  myResults[[r]] <- fit # save results
} # end for loop

length(myResults) # check length

# graph chi-square values
chisqs <- NULL
for(r in 1:nReps){
  chisqs <- c(chisqs,
              lavInspect(myResults[[r]], what='test')$standard$stat)
} # end for loop
hist(chisqs)

The start values are also stored inside the fit objects.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.

messages.subject_clean: Regressing slope on intercept in multivariate growth curve model
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I'm running a multivariate growth model with two variables measured across 3 waves.

Here's the model specification I'm using, with non-uniform time differences. Two variables here are "cyn" and "cms".

model.cms.cynic <- "
icyn =~ 1*T1_Cynic + 1*T2_Cynic + 1*T3_Cynic
scyn =~ 0*T1_Cynic + 1*T2_Cynic + 5.8*T3_Cynic

icms =~ 1*T1_CMS + 1*T2_CMS + 1*T3_CMS
scms =~ 0*T1_CMS + 1*T2_CMS + 5.8*T3_CMS

scyn ~ icms
scms ~ icyn
"
I was interested in looking at 1) associations between the two intercepts, 2) associations between the two slopes, and 3) whether an intercept for one variable predicts the slope of another variable.

My first question is whether the last two lines of my code adequately test my third research question.

My second question pertains to the results I got for the third question in tandem with the associations I found for the first two questions.

The results showed that the intercept of cms ("icms") negatively predicted the slope of cyn ("scyn"). That said, because I also observed that icms and icyn were positively associated, I'm not sure whether predicting the slope of cms from the intercept of cyn needs to also control for the intercept of cms, since

1) higher icms predicted higher icyn,
2) higher icyn would restrict the growth of cyn (=scyn) due to ceiling effect, which would
3) contribute to the observed negative coefficient of icms predicting scyn (which could be considered as an artifact).

Is this reasoning correct, or unfounded? Does the growth curve model (based on my specification) take that ceiling effect into account already?

Please let me know if you would like to see the full estimate results.

Regards,
Sangmin

messages.body_plain:
For what it is worth, you might to consider the fact that there exists a linear slope intercept growth model for both of these processes which has a zero correlation between the intercept and slope factors. To see this, specify the random intercept as you have done, but freely estimate the t1_cynic and t1_cms loadings, freely estimate the t3_cynic and t3_cms loadings, and constraing the t2 loadints of both values to be the amount of elapsed time between the t1 and t3 freely estimated loadings. The slope factor loadings for both factors should be fixed to 1. This will then let you estimate correlations between the two intercept factors, the two slope factors, and the covariances between the intercept factor of icyn and slope factor of xcms as well as the covariance o ficms and scyn. FWIW. Phil

Karla

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm fitting a model where I set a number of path coefficients to be equal across groups. When I look at the summary the estimates are equal but the standardized values are not. I understand that standardized coefficients can vary even among constrained paths because they are calculated on a per group basis because of the difference in variances among groups.

So, how do I report my results in a path diagram? I want to show a unique value for all groups for those paths that I fixed to an equal coefficient and be able to compare effects within and across groups.

Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: Standardized coefficients vary when set to be equal
messages.subject_clean: Standardized coefficients vary when set to be equal
messages.body_plain:
This question is an interesting one, though not an easy one. I would love to see more discussion on this topic.

Anyway, let me share my two cents.

I use a 1-predictor regression for illustration.

y ~ x

Let:
The variance of x, x~~x, be v_x.
The coefficient of x to y be B.
The *error* variance of y, y~~y, be ev_y.

The variance of y, v_y, is not a parameter, but is equal to (B^2)v_x + ev_y.

The standardized coefficient of x to y (with std.all), beta, is then B*sqrt(v_x/v_y) = B*sqrt(v_x/((B^2)v_x + ev_y)

So, for a multiple-group model, as you already found, it is possible that even if a regression coefficient is constrained to be equal across groups, the standardized coefficients are still different across groups. In this simple scenario, the standardized coefficient depends on (is a function of) *three* parameters, not one. Even if the (unstandardized) coefficient are the same, differences in the variance of the predictor and the error variance of outcome can result in different standardized coefficients, unless sqrt(v_x/((B^2)v_x + ev_y) is also the same across group.

Things get much more complicated when there are more than one predictor for a dependent variable.

This is an illustration in lavaan:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-15
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
dat <- HolzingerSwineford1939
dat$x <- dat$x1
dat$y <- dat$x4
mod <-
"
y ~ c(B1, B2) * x
x ~~ c(v_x1, v_x2) * x
y ~~ c(ev_y1, ev_y2) * y
v_y1 := (B1^2) * v_x1 + ev_y1
v_y2 := (B2^2) * v_x2 + ev_y2
B1 == B2
beta1 := B1 * sqrt(v_x1 / v_y1)
beta2 := B2 * sqrt(v_x2 / v_y2)
"
fit <- sem(mod, data = dat, group = "school")
est <- parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE, ci = FALSE, se = FALSE)
est
#>      lhs op                rhs block group label   est std.lv <http://std.lv> std.all std.nox
#> 1      y  ~                  x     1     1    B1 0.373  0.373   0.389   0.389
#> 2      x ~~                  x     1     1  v_x1 1.395  1.395   1.000   1.000
#> 3      y ~~                  y     1     1 ev_y1 1.090  1.090   0.849   0.849
#> 4      y ~1                        1     1       0.979  0.979   0.864   0.864
#> 5      x ~1                        1     1       4.941  4.941   4.183   4.183
#> 6      y  ~                  x     2     2    B2 0.373  0.373   0.376   0.376
#> 7      x ~~                  x     2     2  v_x2 1.319  1.319   1.000   1.000
#> 8      y ~~                  y     2     2 ev_y2 1.113  1.113   0.858   0.858
#> 9      y ~1                        2     2       1.478  1.478   1.298   1.298
#> 10     x ~1                        2     2       4.930  4.930   4.293   4.293
#> 11  v_y1 :=  (B1^2)*v_x1+ev_y1     0     0  v_y1 1.284  1.284   1.000   1.000
#> 12  v_y2 :=  (B2^2)*v_x2+ev_y2     0     0  v_y2 1.296  1.296   1.000   1.000
#> 14 beta1 := B1*sqrt(v_x1/v_y1)     0     0 beta1 0.389  0.389   0.389   0.389
#> 15 beta2 := B2*sqrt(v_x2/v_y2)     0     0 beta2 0.376  0.376   0.376   0.376

# Compare the lavaan std.all values and user-defined values
est[c(1, 6, 13, 14), ]
#>      lhs op                rhs block group label   est std.lv <http://std.lv> std.all std.nox
#> 1      y  ~                  x     1     1    B1 0.373  0.373   0.389   0.389
#> 6      y  ~                  x     2     2    B2 0.373  0.373   0.376   0.376
#> 14 beta1 := B1*sqrt(v_x1/v_y1)     0     0 beta1 0.389  0.389   0.389   0.389
#> 15 beta2 := B2*sqrt(v_x2/v_y2)     0     0 beta2 0.376  0.376   0.376   0.376
No simple solution, and also nothing wrong with this phenomenon.

Assuming the error variance is also constrained to be the same, then the only parameter that can lead to the discrepancy between B and "beta" in the model above is the variance of x. So, even if the unstandardized effect of x is the same across group, a group difference in the variances, and so the SDs, of x certainly should lead to a difference in "beta" because "one SD increase of x" does not mean the same increase in x in its original unit across group.

But there is a possible solution. Constrain more parameters to be the same across groups. In the example above, if we also constrain the variances and the error variances to be equal across group, then both Bs and betas will be the same across groups (guarantee to be the same):
mod2 <-
"
y ~ c(B, B) * x
x ~~ c(v_x, v_x) * x
y ~~ c(ev_y, ev_y) * y
"
fit2 <- sem(mod2, data = dat, group = "school")
est2 <- parameterEstimates(fit2, standardized = TRUE, ci = FALSE, se = FALSE)
est2
#>    lhs op rhs block group label   est std.lv <http://std.lv> std.all std.nox
#> 1    y  ~   x     1     1     B 0.373  0.373   0.382   0.382
#> 2    x ~~   x     1     1   v_x 1.358  1.358   1.000   1.000
#> 3    y ~~   y     1     1  ev_y 1.101  1.101   0.854   0.854
#> 4    y ~1         1     1       0.981  0.981   0.864   0.864
#> 5    x ~1         1     1       4.941  4.941   4.240   4.240
#> 6    y  ~   x     2     2     B 0.373  0.373   0.382   0.382
#> 7    x ~~   x     2     2   v_x 1.358  1.358   1.000   1.000
#> 8    y ~~   y     2     2  ev_y 1.101  1.101   0.854   0.854
#> 9    y ~1         2     2       1.480  1.480   1.303   1.303
#> 10   x ~1         2     2       4.930  4.930   4.230   4.230
I rarely see researchers do this. The suggestion by Keith is much more common. Nevertheless, empirically, a model like this is possible. If you really want to have some unstandardized and standardized path coefficients to be the same across groups, and your data supports a model like this one, and you have theoretical reasons to fit this model, then I see no reason why you cannot try.

My two cents.

Regards,
Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝)

If your model is a big one, it may not be easy to ensure that two programs really fit the same model, due to possible differences in some default settings.

You used FIML to handle missing. Just to make sure that Mplus and lavaan really fit the same model, how about turning off FIML in both Mplus and lavaan, to see if they have similar results when fitting the model to complete data?

If they yield similar results, then the difference may be due to FIML. I sometimes also encounter problems in fitting a model with FIML, especially when the sample sizes is large.

By the way, if you are not going to replicate things using 0.6-13, you can consider updating lavaan to 0.6-15. It may not be related but it does no harm to update, just in case.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I am struggling to understand the parameterization of the lavaan output when using categorical manifest variables. I would like to start this question by first showing with continuous indicators the part which I understand, and then with categorical indicators the part which I don't understand.

Continuous indicators

For continuous indicators, let's use this script to manually generate the data and analyze it with lavaan:

trait <- rnorm(500)

error1 <- rnorm(500)
error2 <- rnorm(500)
error3 <- rnorm(500)
error4 <- rnorm(500)

X1 <- 1.1*trait + error1
X2 <- 1.3*trait + error2
X3 <- 1.5*trait + error3
X4 <- 1.7*trait + error4

data <- cbind(X1, X2, X3, X4)

model <- '
X =~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4
X ~~ X
'

fit <- cfa(model, data, std.lv <http://std.lv> = T)

summary(fit)

This is the output:

Latent Variables:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
  X =~
    X1                1.126    0.059   19.126    0.000
    X2                1.349    0.064   21.081    0.000
    X3                1.544    0.067   23.129    0.000
    X4                1.763    0.076   23.057    0.000

Variances:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    X                 1.000
   .X1                0.954    0.071   13.350    0.000
   .X2                0.967    0.079   12.274    0.000
   .X3                0.842    0.081   10.403    0.000
   .X4                1.114    0.106   10.485    0.000

So as you can see, the values in the output closely match the values in the data generation. In the data generation, I have set the values of the factor loadings to be 1.1, 1.3, 1.5 and 1.7 and lavaan succesfully estimated them to be 1.13, 1.35, 1.54 and 1.76.

Catrgorical indicators

For this we will use almost exactly the same script, but we will just add the part where we convert the continuous manifest variables to binary ones by setting some chosen threshold and using the if function to see if the value is larger than that threshold.

trait <- rnorm(500)

error1 <- rnorm(500)
error2 <- rnorm(500)
error3 <- rnorm(500)
error4 <- rnorm(500)

X1 <- 1.1*trait + error1
X2 <- 1.3*trait + error2
X3 <- 1.5*trait + error3
X4 <- 1.7*trait + error4

X1 <- as.numeric(X1 > -1.3)
X2 <- as.numeric(X2 > -0.6)
X3 <- as.numeric(X3 > 1.4)
X4 <- as.numeric(X4 > 2.1)

model <- '
X =~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4
X ~~ X
'

data <- cbind(X1, X2, X3, X4)

fit <- cfa(model, data, std.lv <http://std.lv> = T, ordered = c("X1", "X2", "X3", "X4"))

summary(fit)

Let's now look at the output:

Latent Variables:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
  X =~
    X1                0.730    0.067   10.854    0.000
    X2                0.812    0.062   13.143    0.000
    X3                0.794    0.055   14.422    0.000
    X4                0.898    0.058   15.520    0.000

Intercepts:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
   .X1                0.000
   .X2                0.000
   .X3                0.000
   .X4                0.000
    X                 0.000

Thresholds:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    X1|t1            -0.813    0.063  -12.829    0.000
    X2|t1            -0.353    0.057   -6.152    0.000
    X3|t1             0.793    0.063   12.580    0.000
    X4|t1             1.146    0.072   15.962    0.000

Variances:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    X                 1.000
   .X1                0.466
   .X2                0.340
   .X3                0.370
   .X4                0.194

Scales y*:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    X1                1.000
    X2                1.000
    X3                1.000
    X4                1.000

This time the values in the output do not seem to closely match the factor loading specified in the data generating script. Also, the same thing applies to the thresholds. They also seem to be quite far off from the values in the data generation.

However, I believe that the model wasn't badly estimated, but just that it uses different parameterization when dealing with categorical variables.

I can't figure out how to convert from one parameterization to another, though. And I really need to do this because I am setting up a simulation study and if the parameters aren't on the same scale, then there is no way for me to assess the bias of the model. Can anyone provide formulae which would allow me to convert between the two parameterizations.

Or if the problem is something else and I am understanding this wrong, please let me know what my mistake is and how can I correct it. Many thanks!

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-15
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.

set.seed(870431)
n <- 50000

trait <- rnorm(n)

error1 <- rnorm(n)
error2 <- rnorm(n)
error3 <- rnorm(n)
error4 <- rnorm(n)

X1 <- 1.1*trait + error1
X2 <- 1.3*trait + error2
X3 <- 1.5*trait + error3
X4 <- 1.7*trait + error4

X1 <- as.numeric(X1 > -1.3)
X2 <- as.numeric(X2 > -0.6)
X3 <- as.numeric(X3 > 1.4)
X4 <- as.numeric(X4 > 2.1)

model <- '
X =~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4
X ~~ X
'

data <- cbind(X1, X2, X3, X4)

fit <- cfa(model, data, std.lv <http://std.lv> = T, ordered = c("X1", "X2", "X3", "X4"))

# Verify that the loadings are equal to the standardized loadings
est <- subset(parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE), op == "=~")
est

#> 1   X =~  X1 0.746 0.006 116.278      0    0.733    0.758  0.746   0.746

messages.body_plain:
1) Where does the formula for the original standardized loading come from? I thought that the formula is supposed to be original_loading * sqrt(trait_variance) / sqrt(item_variance).

You are right. I omitted the trait variance because it is one in the population (and I am lazy). Sorry for the confusion caused. (This is also why I used "sqrt(loading_original^2 + 1)", not the usual form but I made use of the convenient fact that all error variances are equal to 1.)

> 2) Is the same method used to make the thresholds standardized?

I think so. I rarely interpret the thresholds. Using the same example in my previous post, the population thresholds with X1 to X4 standardized and the results from lavaan are pretty close.
# Check threshold
est_t <- subset(parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE), op == "|")
est_t

#>   lhs op rhs    est    se        z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper std.lv <http://std.lv> std.all

#> 6  X1  |  t1 -0.874 0.006 -135.318      0   -0.886   -0.861 -0.874  -0.874
#> 7  X2  |  t1 -0.357 0.006  -62.206      0   -0.368   -0.346 -0.357  -0.357
#> 8  X3  |  t1  0.774 0.006  123.703      0    0.762    0.787  0.774   0.774
#> 9  X4  |  t1  1.066 0.007  153.786      0    1.052    1.079  1.066   1.066
#>   std.nox
#> 6  -0.874
#> 7  -0.357
#> 8   0.774
#> 9   1.066
# Population thresholds with Xs standardized
threshold_original <- c(-1.3, -0.6, 1.4, 2.1)
sd_x <- sqrt(loading_original^2 + 1)
round(threshold_original / sd_x, 3)
#> [1] -0.874 -0.366  0.777  1.065
round(est_t$est, 3)
#> [1] -0.874 -0.357  0.774  1.066
(I only included the new lines. Please combine the code above with that in the previous post to reproduce the results.)

Regards,
Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝)

messages.subject_clean: Different parameterization when using categorical items
messages.body_plain:
AM,
Maybe this was clear from the context but I thought that it might be helpful to point out why your thresholds were scaled differently.  The parameterization used by lavaan scales the unobserved continuous indicators as z scores.  You simulated them as the sum of two z scores.  The sum of two z scores will not itself be distributed as a z score when the two component z scores are orthogonal.  The variance will be 2.  Your simulated continuous indicator variable is a composite.  The variance of a composite is the sum of the covariance matrix of its component variables.  This is why Shu Fai suggested looking at the standardized estimates.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Sil,
I hesitate to post again on this thread because I do not fully understand your question.  However, perhaps it is helpful to point out that it is no longer considered adequate reporting to report only standardized estimates.  The reason is that these will be misleading to the reader if the groups differ in the variances of the variables.  As such, it is considered best practices to always report the raw estimates possibly supplemented with standardized estimates.

On one interpretation of your question, you already have what you describe wanting:  You constrained the raw estimates to be equal so reporting those on the path diagram would give you one number that applies to all the groups.

An important point from Shu Fai's post is the proviso that the data supports the model.  If the raw estimates are the same in every group and the groups differ in variances, then these two premises jointly imply that the standardized estimates are not equal.  So, asking for equal standardized estimates under those conditions is asking for something that is not there to be found.

You may wish to consider methods of presentation other than a path diagram.  For example, if you reported the effect size estimates in a Cleveland dot plot you could put each effect in a different row and provide a separate point in each row for each group, surrounded by an error bar representing the confidence interval.  Alternatively, you may wish to consider a tabular presentation.  Path diagrams tend to work best for relatively simple models.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
