messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to calculate the HTMT for constructs labeled G->V below. My problem is that when I run the code below, I get the following error message: Error in htmt(DNT.Single.Level.CFA.1aaa, data = d__, sample.cov = NULL,  : Missing observed variables in the dataset: G S F V P N

After inspecting my code, the error made sense, as I am running a hierarchical CFA and the second order latent factors (Net_Motiv & Net_Resis) use the latent factors of G S F V P N as indicators, so they do not exist as observed variables in my data set. Does anyone know if it's possible to write the HTMT argument such that it applies this analysis only to the first order latent factors? I spent some time trying to do so, but have yet to find a solution. The analysis worked just fine when I deleted "Net_Motiv=~G+S+F, Net_Resis=~V+P+N" from the code, but it seems odd to me to run a new CFA in order to calculate the HTMT results of the hierarchical CFA that will be reported in my paper.

Any help would be greatly appreciated!!

Relevant code:
Model.CFA <- '
G=~G_item_1+G_item_2+G_item_3+G_item_4
S=~S_item_1+S_item_2+S_item_3+S_item_4
F=~F_item_1+F_item_2+F_item_3+F_item_4
P=~P_item_1+P_item_2+P_item_3+P_item_4
N=~N_item_1+N_item_2+N_item_3+N_item_4
R=~R_item_1+R_item_2+R_item_3+R_item_4
V=~V_item_1+V_item_2+V_item_3+V_item_4
Net_Motiv=~G+S+F
Net_Resis=~V+P+N'
set.seed(62973)
fModel.CFA <- cfa(Model.CFA=d__, se="robust.sem", estimator = 'MLM', bootstrap=2000)
summary(fModel.CFA, fit.measures= T,standardized=T,  rsquare=T)
htmt(Model.CFA, data=d__,  sample.cov=NULL, ordered=NULL, absolute=TRUE)

messages.subject_clean: HTMT calculation with only a subset of your latent factors?
messages.body_plain:
As long as you apply "=~", the HTMT function understands this as a factor measured by observed variables. See the first lines of code: https://rdrr.io/cran/semTools/src/R/htmt.R
>From a purely technical point of view, you can get around this by modifying the line "factors <- unique(model$lhs)". Something like this:

body(htmt)[[4]] <- substitute(
  factors <- na.omit(sapply(unique(model$lhs), function(x, model) {
    if(TRUE %in% sapply(model[model$lhs == x, "rhs"], function(y, ov) y %in% ov, lavNames(model, "ov"))) x else NA
  }, model))
)

Caution. It is of course a bad practice to hack the source code ... You will also get the same results if you use the syntax for the CFA without the 2nd order structure and pass it to the HTMT function. Additionally, there are quite a few criticisms on HTMT.

HTH

messages.subject: Sequence of nested models to test for measurement invariance of categorical items
messages.subject_clean: Sequence of nested models to test for measurement invariance of categorical items
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaaners,

I have a dataset consisting of 30 ordered categorical indicators (2-5 response categories) measured at two timepoints (60 items in total). EFA conducted on each time point separately suggests a solution of 3 factors (7-11 items loading on to each factor).

I now want to test the 3-factor structure for measurement invariance using Wu and Estabrook's (2016) method for categorical indicators. I have read their article and the measeq.syntax example syntax.

>From my understanding, I would first set up the configural model:
config.syntax <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = config.mod,
                               data = complete(MI2, action = 1),
                               parameterization = 'theta',
                               ID.fac = 'std.lv <http://std.lv>',
                               ID.cat = 'Wu.Estabrook.2016',
                               longFacNames = list(
                                 slp = c('slp1', 'slp2'),
                                 dep = c('dep1', 'dep2'),
                                 man = c('man1', 'man2')
                               )) %>%
  as.character()

Then, as per Wu and Estabrook, I would set thresholds equal across timepoints before testing other forms of invariance:
thresh.syntax <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = config.mod,
                               data = complete(MI2, action = 1),
                               parameterization = 'theta',
                               ID.fac = 'std.lv <http://std.lv>',
                               ID.cat = 'Wu.Estabrook.2016',
                               longFacNames = list(                                                slp = c('slp1', 'slp2'),
                                 dep = c('dep1', 'dep2'),
                                 man = c('man1', 'man2'),
                               long.equal = c("thresholds")
                               )) %>%
  as.character()

However, it is unclear to me which model(s) to test next, among the following:
long.equal = c("thresholds", "loadings")
long.equal = c("thresholds", "intercepts")
long.equal = c("thresholds", "loadings", "intercepts")
long.equal =  c("thresholds", "loadings", "intercepts", "residuals")
I have avoided using names (weak, metric, scalar, strong, strict etc) as these seem more relevant for continuous indicators.

Any guidance would be much appreciated!

messages.subject: Re: RMSEA 90% CI
messages.subject_clean: RMSEA 90% CI
messages.body_plain:
> why does lavaan report RMSEA CI at the 90% and not at the 95%?

A hypothesis of (not-)close fit is a directional hypothesis.
H0: ε < .05 (close fit)
H0: ε > .05 (not-close fit)
A two-tailed test with alpha = .10 has the same tail probabilities / critical values as a one-tailed test in either direction.  So the 2 confidence limits of a two-tailed 90% CI give you the single 95% confidence limit for either test (close or not-close fit).

MacCallum, R. C., Browne, M. W., & Sugawara, H. M. (1996). Power analysis and determination of sample size for covariance structure modeling. Psychological Methods, 1(2), 130–149. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.1.2.130

MacCallum, R. C., Browne, M. W., & Cai, L. (2006). Testing differences between nested covariance structure models: Power analysis and null hypotheses. Psychological Methods, 11(1), 19–35. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.11.1.19

The same is provided for CRMR or SRMR from lavResiduals(), although it is not explicitly labeled as 90%.  The unbiased estimates (e.g., usrmr) are also provided.

Maydeu-Olivares, A. (2017). Assessing the size of model misfit in structural equation models. Psychometrika, 82(3), 533–558. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9552-7

If you want a different alpha / confidence level, then you can set it with lavaan::fitMeasures(..., fm=)

> HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
+               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
+               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
>
> fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
> fitMeasures(fit, c("rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower","rmsea.ci.upper"))
         rmsea rmsea.ci.lower rmsea.ci.upper
         0.092          0.071          0.114
> ## for 99% confidence, request a 98% CI
> fitMeasures(fit, c("rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower","rmsea.ci.upper"),
>             fm = list(rmsea.ci.level = 0.98))
         rmsea rmsea.ci.lower rmsea.ci.upper
         0.092          0.062          0.122

The p values can also be determined for a designated H0, using the fm= elements shown on the ?fitMeasures help page.  I don't think you can request different alpha / confidence level from lavResiduals(),  but it is a normal-theory CI, so it would be easy to construct it yourself from the SE provided.

Terrence D. Jorgensen    (he, him, his)
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Different parameterization when using categorical items
messages.subject_clean: Different parameterization when using categorical items
messages.body_plain:
To expand on what Keith wrote, you generated independent normal trait and errors with SD = variance = 1, so indeed each indicator's total variance = 1 + 1 = 2.  But if the an error had been correlated with the trait, then the total variance would include the covariance s_12:  1 + 1 + 2*s_12.  This is a linear-algebra result, if you want to look further into that.

When you discretized them with thresholds c(-1.3, -0.6, 1.4, 2.1), those were applied to normal distributions with mean = 0 and sd = sqrt(2), which can be visualized like so:

curve(dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(2)), from = -6, to = 6)
abline(v = c(-1.3, -0.6, 1.4, 2.1))

If you intended those to be standardized thresholds (z scores), then you would have to apply the z-score formula: subtract the mean (0) and divide by the SD:

## Same graph, only x-axis scale changes:
zThresh <- c(-1.3, -0.6, 1.4, 2.1) / sqrt(2)
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = 1), from = -3, to = 3)
abline(v = zThresh)

So the parameterization is arbitrary, but using standardized thresholds would have to be applied to standard-normal variables (i.e., with total variance = 1, not 2).  That would require setting loadings to be < 1, and setting your error variances to be 1 minus the explained variance (i.e., lambda * psi * lambda).  Because your factor variance is 1, the explained variance is reduced to lambda^2, so error variances should be 1 - lambda^2 to simulate standard-normal indicators.  For example:

error1 <- rnorm(500, sd = sqrt(1 - loading1^2))

> still confused by the term  sqrt(loading_original^2 + 1)  Would someone be so kind to write out how this term is created by simplifying from some more general term?

That follows from above.  When you use the theta parameterization, you are setting (by default) the residual variances of latent responses to be 1.  Because that's what your population values happened to be, using parameterization = "theta" would be consistent with your population.  In this case, the explained variance is still lambda^2, and the residual / unexplained variance is 1, so the total variance is the sum of those 2 (and the SD is the square-root of that).

A second option is to use delta parameterization, but make the output in your original post comparable to your population parameters by applying a different identification constraint on the total variance of latent responses y*.  You can specify the scaling factors with the ~*~ operator, which is 1 / SD.  By default, that is 1 in the default delta parameterization, but you could update it to be consistent with your population by setting it to 1 / sqrt(2) = 0.7071068:

model <- '
X =~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4

X1 ~*~ 0.7071068*X1
X2 ~*~ 0.7071068*X2
X3 ~*~ 0.7071068*X3
X4 ~*~ 0.7071068*X4
'

messages.subject: Re: Odd property of lavaan with nonlinear constraints
messages.subject_clean: Odd property of lavaan with nonlinear constraints
messages.body_plain:
> This involves putting nonlinear constraints on the loadings

That's not what your syntax does.  You are defining new parameters using the ":=" operator.  lavaan should probably give an error when you define a new parameter with the same name as an existing one, but that is why you have a different L1 etc. among the estimates and among the defined (functions of other) estimates.

To set a constraint, use the "==" operator:

L1 == ...

> The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov) does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue (= 7.339558e-14) is close to zero. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

This is not about the covariance matrix of data, but about the estimated parameters.  It happens when there is multicollinearity among estimated parameters, which I imagine can happen when some parameters are functions of others.  This happens all the time when a dummy code's mean and variance are both estimated, since the variance is a function of the mean.

Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Donnerstag, 30. März 2023 um 11:06:53 UTC+2:
> > why does lavaan report RMSEA CI at the 90% and not at the 95%?
>
> A hypothesis of (not-)close fit is a directional hypothesis.
> H0: ε < .05 (close fit)
> H0: ε > .05 (not-close fit)
> A two-tailed test with alpha = .10 has the same tail probabilities / critical values as a one-tailed test in either direction.  So the 2 confidence limits of a two-tailed 90% CI give you the single 95% confidence limit for either test (close or not-close fit).
>
> MacCallum, R. C., Browne, M. W., & Sugawara, H. M. (1996). Power analysis and determination of sample size for covariance structure modeling. Psychological Methods, 1(2), 130–149. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.1.2.130
>
> MacCallum, R. C., Browne, M. W., & Cai, L. (2006). Testing differences between nested covariance structure models: Power analysis and null hypotheses. Psychological Methods, 11(1), 19–35. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.11.1.19
>
>
> The same is provided for CRMR or SRMR from lavResiduals(), although it is not explicitly labeled as 90%.  The unbiased estimates (e.g., usrmr) are also provided.
>
> Maydeu-Olivares, A. (2017). Assessing the size of model misfit in structural equation models. Psychometrika, 82(3), 533–558. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9552-7
>
>
> If you want a different alpha / confidence level, then you can set it with lavaan::fitMeasures(..., fm=)
>
> > HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
> +               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
> +               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
> >
> > fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
> > fitMeasures(fit, c("rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower","rmsea.ci.upper"))
>          rmsea rmsea.ci.lower rmsea.ci.upper
>          0.092          0.071          0.114
> > ## for 99% confidence, request a 98% CI
> > fitMeasures(fit, c("rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower","rmsea.ci.upper"),
> >             fm = list(rmsea.ci.level = 0.98))
>          rmsea rmsea.ci.lower rmsea.ci.upper
>          0.092          0.062          0.122
>
> The p values can also be determined for a designated H0, using the fm= elements shown on the ?fitMeasures help page.  I don't think you can request different alpha / confidence level from lavResiduals(),  but it is a normal-theory CI, so it would be easy to construct it yourself from the SE provided.
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for that Terrence, your help is always much appreciated.

A small follow-up question, so I can better understand the syntax. Say I generate measEq.syntax for two levels of measurement invariance, e.g.
long.equal = c("thresholds") vs.

long.equal = c("thresholds", "loadings")

As expected, the first model constrains only the thresholds, while the second model constrains thresholds and item loadings.

However, what I find interesting is that syntax 2 also releases some constraints which are present in syntax 1. Specifically, syntax 2 allows all common factor variances at the second occasion to be freely estimated.

Comparing a subset of the syntax (highlighted are the lines of syntax which differ between the two):

     ## COMMON-FACTOR VARIANCES:

slp1 ~~ 1*slp1 + psi.1_1*slp1
slp2 ~~ 1*slp2 + psi.2_2*slp2
dep1 ~~ 1*dep1 + psi.3_3*dep1
dep2 ~~ 1*dep2 + psi.4_4*dep2
man1 ~~ 1*man1 + psi.5_5*man1
man2 ~~ 1*man2 + psi.6_6*man2

  ## COMMON-FACTOR VARIANCES:

slp1 ~~ 1*slp1 + psi.1_1*slp1
slp2 ~~ NA*slp2 + psi.2_2*slp2
dep1 ~~ 1*dep1 + psi.3_3*dep1
dep2 ~~ NA*dep2 + psi.4_4*dep2
man1 ~~ 1*man1 + psi.5_5*man1
man2 ~~ NA*man2 + psi.6_6*man2
My understanding of measurement invariance (which is admittedly, quite elementary) is that when testing increasingly strict levels of invariance, constraints are added and not released.

So why is it the case that when going from 1 > 2, certain constraints are released?
N.B. I have also noticed this behaviour when comparing long.equal = c("thresholds", "loadings") with  long.equal = c("thresholds", "loadings", "intercepts")syntax.

Thanks
